title: BlackRock Says India Has Been 'Over-Punished' by Global Markets. It Thinks the Worst of the Selling Is Over.
excerpt: Record foreign outflows of $30 billion, a 27 per cent IT crash, and a war-driven oil spike have hammered Indian equities in 2026. But the world's largest asset manager says the rotation has gone too far — and India's absence from the AI trade may be its advantage.
body:
Two of the world's most influential institutional voices have converged on the same message this week: India's stock market has been punished too hard, and the worst may be over.

BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager with over $14 trillion under management, said India's equity market had been "over-punished" for lacking a direct AI play and for its vulnerability to higher oil prices. Lighthouse Canton, a global wealth management firm with more than $5 billion in assets, went further — calling India's absence from the AI semiconductor frenzy an "advantage of absence" that investors were only beginning to appreciate.

The calls come at a moment when India's market numbers look brutal. The Nifty 50 and Sensex are down roughly 11 per cent and 13 per cent so far in 2026. The IT index has cratered 27 per cent on fears of AI-led disruption to outsourcing. Foreign investors have pulled out a record $30 billion from Indian equities this year, redirecting capital to South Korea and Taiwan — markets dominated by the semiconductor and memory chip names that have defined the AI trade.

South Korea and Taiwan have both overtaken India in total market capitalisation in the past month.

## The 'Advantage of Absence'

Abhay Laijawala, chief investment officer for India at Lighthouse Canton, told Reuters on Friday that the concentration in AI-adjacent chip stocks in East Asian markets had reached levels where investors were "fatally underpricing" risks.

South Korea and Taiwan have both begun to see foreign outflows in June, he noted, suggesting investors have started trimming crowded positions.

India, by contrast, has little exposure to chip fabrication. But it offers a deep, listed universe tied to the next wave of AI-driven capital expenditure — power infrastructure, data centres, electrical equipment, cooling systems, engineering, and capital goods.

"We have plenty of picks and shovels," Laijawala said, using the gold rush metaphor for the companies that supply the tools rather than mine the gold themselves.

## BlackRock's Conviction

Natasha Sarkaria, EMEA investment strategy lead for wealth at BlackRock, told Reuters earlier this week that India remained one of the firm's "highest-conviction, medium- to long-term emerging-market trades," supported by demographics, infrastructure spending, financials, and indirect AI-linked opportunities.

"As long as India's GDP grows between 6 per cent and 7 per cent, that's a nice sweet spot for the economy to keep growing, keep expanding," Sarkaria said. India's economy grew a stronger-than-expected 7.8 per cent in the March quarter.

BlackRock is positioned "constructively" on India rather than an outright overweight, Sarkaria added — an institutional distinction that signals confidence without chasing the current downturn.

The firm acknowledged the headwinds. India's earlier "Goldilocks" mix of benign inflation and strong growth has been disrupted by the Iran war, which pushed Brent crude above $90 a barrel for months, pressured the rupee to record lows, and raised the risk of wider supply shocks. India is the world's third-largest oil importer.

But, Sarkaria said, "the rotation has gone too far."

## What It Means for NRI Investors

The institutional reassessment lands at a moment when India is actively courting diaspora capital. The Reserve Bank of India announced this month that it will bear the full hedging cost for three- to five-year foreign currency non-resident deposits, a move that prompted HDFC Bank, State Bank of India, and AU Small Finance Bank to hike NRI dollar deposit rates by as much as 300 basis points.

Separately, the government amended its FEMA rules this week to allow all individuals resident outside India — not just NRIs and OCI holders — to buy and sell listed Indian securities on a repatriation basis. The pool of eligible investors has expanded dramatically.

Analysts estimate banks could raise $35 billion to $40 billion through the NRI deposit scheme alone by September.

Kotak Mahindra Asset Management's chief investment officer Harsha Upadhyaya struck a cautiously optimistic note: "Now that India's valuations have become reasonable, foreign flows could return once the current geopolitical uncertainty settles, though the timing remains uncertain."

The Iran deal — which Trump says could be signed as early as Sunday — would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and collapse crude prices. If it materialises, the single largest macro headwind facing Indian equities evaporates overnight.

For NRI investors who have watched their India exposure shrink all year, the question is shifting from whether to re-enter to when. Two of the world's sharpest institutional investors are saying: the worst is likely behind you.

nri_angle: NRI investors who pulled money out of Indian equities — or watched their India-linked portfolios shrink — are now being told by two major institutional players that the selloff has overshot. With the RBI sweetening NRI deposit rates and India opening its stock market to all foreigners, the diaspora has new reasons to look again.
author: Diaspora Desk
